Every spring the snowmelt comes down from the mountains and the men who manage the canals begin their long argument about how to divide it. The valley has been farmed for three thousand years, and the irrigation ditches follow lines that were cut before anyone kept written records. In a dry year the argument is about survival; in a wet year it is about custom. The engineers who built the first modern dam promised that the water would be shared fairly, and for two decades it was. Then the orchards came, and with the orchards the demand for water rose faster than anyone had planned.
The old families still hold the land closest to the head of the canal, which means they take their share first whether the year is wet or dry. Further down, the smaller holdings depend on what is left, and in the summer of a bad year it can be very little. A survey carried out by the regional office found that the fields at the tail of the canal received, on average, less than a third of the water that reached the fields at the top, and that the difference had been growing since the orchards were planted.
There is no simple remedy. Lining the ditches with concrete saves water but costs money that the smallholders do not have, and the big landowners see no reason to pay for a change that would mainly benefit their neighbours. Metering the canals sounds fair until one asks who will read the meters and how the reading will be enforced. The courts have been asked to settle the question twice in the last forty years, and both times they have ruled that custom governs, which is another way of saying that nothing changes.
Last winter a consulting firm presented a plan that would consolidate the three water boards into a single authority, with a single schedule of allocation and a single budget for repairs. The plan was praised by the newspapers and quietly buried by the boards, each of which feared that consolidation would cost it its own seat at the table. The chairman of the upper board, whose family has farmed the head of the canal since the nineteenth century, remarked that he had seen many plans in his lifetime and that the water had outlasted all of them.
Meanwhile, the towns at the mouth of the valley have grown, and the water they draw has begun to matter as much as the water the fields draw. Economists who study the area note that the tourism industry now employs more people than the mills did at their height, and that developers from the Middle East have bought several thousand acres along the northern canal. The new owners have replaced the old flood irrigation with drip lines and have planted almonds, a crop that pays well and drinks steadily all summer. Whether the smallholders can follow them, and whether the canal can carry enough water for both, is the question the next dry year will answer.
